paper_title: Are Frontier VLM Agents Ready to Be Robot Generalists? An Empirical Study with the Embodied Agent Arena

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A robot generalist must interpret a scene, act on it, and satisfy every condition of a task. How far do frontier vision-language models (VLMs) meet these demands? We introduce Embodied Agent Arena, evaluating ten VLM agents across Geometry, Spatial Reasoning, Affordance, Task Planning, and Manipulation. Its 1,000 cases combine 32 established sources with GeoProbe, our 168-case benchmark for camera, motion, depth, and scale estimation. A minimal harness leaves task decisions to the model through source-native interfaces. Closed-weight models lead all five domains, whereas open-weight VLMs show useful spatial reasoning but substantially lower planning and manipulation success. Beneath these averages, similar geometric errors conceal different scale and shape distortions, and valid region estimates need not identify usable action points. During execution, agents can achieve early subgoals yet lose object control, bind an action to the wrong receiving region, or stop before the required physical state holds. Additional computation does not uniformly resolve these failures: code repair can restore execution without completing the task, while self-review can reverse correct judgments. Failure costs also differ: the strongest planners concentrate failed-token expenditure in prolonged body-control tasks, whereas other models fail broadly across procedures. Matched traces show how successful recovery uses feedback to restore a missing prerequisite and advance the remaining task.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: A robot generalist must turn scene understanding into actions that satisfy complete goal. In an object-placement task, locating the target and grasping it are intermediate steps; success also requires placing it at the specified destination. Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly address spatial relations (Ma et al., 2024, Yang et al., 2024) and action-relevant grounding (Wang et al., 2025a, Song et al., 2024). Learned visuomotor policies connect observations to robot actions (Kim et al., 2024, Black et al., 2024), while language-model controllers select skills or generate executable programs (Ahn et al., 2022, Liang et al., 2022). Perception support and visual action rehearsal further extend these systems (Fu et al., 2026, Guo et al., 2026, Li et al., 2026b, Zhang et al., 2026a). As these systems take on more diverse tasks, the central question becomes: Are frontier VLM agents ready to be robot generalists? Corresponding authors. 1 Haojian Huang et al. Embodied Agent Arena Figure 1. Overview of Embodied Agent Arena. Each row illustrates six tasks in one capability domain, spanning camera and scene estimation, spatial relations, functional grounding, goal-directed planning, and robot manipulation. Fixed-input probes test estimates and judgments; interactive episodes test goal completion. Spatial-tracing overlays show reference paths and 3D target region. Answering this question requires identifying which task requirements remain unsatisfied. For example, trajectory can closely follow reference yet miss its endpoint, while approaching seat and issuing sit action need not establish seated state. Average accuracy can obscure these failures, whereas final failure alone hides achieved subgoals. Evaluation must therefore distinguish prediction accuracy, achieved subgoals, and final task success. To distinguish these requirements systematically, we introduce Embodied Agent Arena, evaluating ten VLM agents across Geometry, Spatial Reasoning, Affordance, Task Planning, and Manipulation (Figure 1). The arena combines established benchmarks with GeoProbe, whose controlled variations in camera motion, object motion, and scale references diagnose geometric estimation. minimal harness retains source interfaces and leaves task decisions to the model. This framework separates metric precision, functional grounding, and native task success, while execution traces identify achieved subgoals and unmet requirements. The comparison shows that closed-weight models lead all five domains, whereas open-weight VLMs complete far fewer Planning and Manipulation tasks. Yet the aggregate gaps conceal distinct errors. Comparable depth errors can arise from common scale bias or from residual distortion; region can overlap the correct functional support while its proposed action point misses that support. Execution makes these distinctions consequential: valid placement can address the outer fixture instead of its basin, and precise gripper motion can leave the object ungrasped. Longer sequences then require maintaining or restoring the physical state on which the next subgoal depends. These findings also explain why additional computation has uneven value. Code repair may restore an admissible program without establishing the required object state, while selfreview can fix coordinate bounds and introduce new relational errors. The costs are similarly structured: for the strongest planners, failed-token expenditure is concentrated in prolonged body-control attempts, whereas other models fail across broader range of procedures. By 2 Haojian Huang et al. Embodied Agent Arena connecting these distributions to matched actionfeedback traces, the arena identifies whether recovery must change target binding, repair prerequisite state, or revise an unsupported claim of task completion. Our contributions are: An evaluation centered on complete task requirements. We evaluate prediction accuracy, functional grounding, subgoal achievement, and final task success across five domains. unified arena with new geometric benchmark, GeoProbe. The 1,000-case arena combines 32 established sources with 168 GeoProbe cases, retaining native operations and success criteria in shared model-directed evaluation framework. diagnosis of task failure after successful intermediate steps. Ten-model comparisons reveal complementary successes and shared failures; traces identify invalid endpoints, unmet goal conditions, and attempts that achieve no further subgoals.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Embodied evaluation has developed along two complementary directions. Control suites measure execution and task transfer (James et al., 2019, Mees et al., 2021, Liu et al., 2023). Varying environments and physical deployment broaden this evaluation to robustness and multiple dimensions of manipulation competence (Chen et al., 2025a, 2026). Visual diagnostics isolate spatial inference (Ma et al., 2024, Yang et al., 2024) and interaction grounding (Song et al., 2024, Qian & Fouhey, 2023). Scene and task question answering (Majumdar et al., 2024, Sermanet et al., 2023) extends this diagnostic view to embodied decisions (Li et al., 2024b, Qi et al., 2025). Scene-linked assessment connects grounding, relational inference, and action to distinguish performance at individual stages from errors propagated between stages (Ruan et al., 2026). As agents undertake longer interactions, final success leaves important aspects of execution unresolved: adherence to constraints (Park et al., 2026), use of relevant history (Luo et al., 2026), and recognition of progress and recovery (Liu et al., 2026). These developments motivate measuring decisions within an episode alongside complete outcomes. The transition from judgment to action depends on where control is represented. Learned policies map observations and instructions directly to actions (Brohan et al., 2023, Zitkovich et al., 2023), with broader task coverage motivating generalist policies (Ghosh et al., 2024, Kim et al., 2024, Black et al., 2024). Language-mediated control instead composes supplied skills (Ahn et al., 2022, Huang et al., 2023b) or executable programs (Liang et al., 2022, Singh et al., 2023); hybrid coordination selects between modular skills and learned policies from the current state (Zhou et al., 2026a). Explicit programs make dependencies (Fu et al., 2026, Du et al., 2025), geometric feedback (Huang et al., 2023a), and reusable interfaces (Li et al., 2026a) available for model-directed composition. Evaluation consequently shifts from the availability of individual actions to the controllers ability to coordinate complete procedure. Composition also requires evidence that remains useful as the scene changes. Visual grounding can fail under physical stress or misleading background cues (Li et al., 2025, Wu et al., 2026, Huang et al., 2026a), motivating methods that repair context and reason over evolving spatial evidence (Huang et al., 2026c, Zhao et al., 2026b,a). Demonstrations supply task context (Jiang et al., 2023, Huang et al., 2026b); retained histories preserve state (Zhang et al., 2026b); verification checks whether execution meets its conditions (Guo et al., 2024, Huang et al., 2026d). 3 Haojian Huang et al. Broader benchmarks bring perception and goal-directed interaction into one evaluation (Yang et al., 2025a, Cheng et al., 2025), extending visual probes toward navigation (Ni et al., 2025, Rasheed et al., 2026) and diverse manipulation tasks (Zhang et al., 2024). Embodied Agent Arena spans metric geometry, spatial inference, functional grounding, planning, and manipulation, with GeoProbe isolating camera, motion, and scale requirements. Its prediction metrics and execution records complement final task success by identifying estimation errors and unsatisfied goal conditions.

sections.title: 3.1 Benchmark Construction and Capability Domains
sections.content: Prediction, grounding, and interactive task success. The arena organizes 1,000 cases from 32 established sources and GeoProbe into five capability domains (Figures 12; Appendix A). Each case specifies observations, query or goal, available operations, and scoring. Geometry, Spatial Reasoning, and Affordance isolate what the agent must estimate or ground; Task Planning and Manipulation test whether decisions produce the required environment state. GeoProbe adds 168 cases that vary camera motion, object motion, and scale references in controlled Blender scenes, complemented by real images. Separating these factors makes it possible to distinguish failure to infer the scene from failure to complete an interaction. Geometry: metric precision and feasibility. Agents estimate intrinsics, pose, depth, dimensions, or displacement from images. InFlux and Map-free test calibration and relative pose (Liang et al., 2025, Arnold et al., 2022); GeoProbe varies camera motion and scale references. TraceSpatial-Bench adds paths on 56 scenes (Zhou et al., 2026b). Trajectory error quantifies path similarity; initiation, arrival, and collision checks test spatial feasibility. 4 Haojian Huang et al. Embodied Agent Arena Figure 2. Construction of the 1,000-case arena. (a) Representative task vocabulary across sources. (b) Five-domain composition, including 112 spatial-tracing cases in Geometry. (c) GeoProbe case counts for calibration, pose, depth, displacement, and scale. (d) Source queries, scenes, and targets form cases for shared agentenvironment loop; state persists between rounds, and native criteria determine termination and scoring. Colors identify domains; logos denote source institutions. Spatial Reasoning: relations and reference frames. Agents infer relations, viewpoints, configurations, and temporal order from images or video (Ma et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2025b, Yang et al., 2024). Comparing object distances, imagining another observers view, and inferring camera motion require different reference-frame transformations. Questions specify the relevant frame and expect category, quantity, or point set. Affordance: contact and functional extent. Agents ground an intended action through contact point or region. UMD tests tool functions such as cutting and scooping (Myers et al., 2015); instructionand action-conditioned 3DOI queries test interaction contacts (Qian & Fouhey, 2023). Point validity checks whether predicted contact point lies inside the reference region. Region IoU measures intersection over union with the reference mask, using native boxes and, separately, direct polygons. Task Planning: satisfying all goal conditions. Agents compose source-provided operations into household, navigation, or scientific procedures (Shridhar et al., 2019, Wang et al., 2022), using visual, textual, or symbolic feedback. Compound goals require several conditions to hold, such as heating an object and placing it at the destination. For terminal state sT and 5 Haojian Huang et al. Manipulation: contact conditions and sequential goals. Agents execute robot motions or skills for placement, insertion, articulation, and coordinated handling (James et al., 2019, Chen et al., 2025a). Language-conditioned variants change the target relation or object (Zhang et al., 2024); sequential tasks require completing ordered subgoals from the states left by preceding actions. Native task success records completion, while condition-level scores expose achieved relations and control events.

sections.title: 3.2 Unified Agent Harness
sections.content: Task decisions remain with the model. The harness provides persistent interaction through each sources observations and operations (Figure 2d). Models interpret observations, select operations, and construct action sequences from feedback. We use native capability to mean these model-directed decisions through the supplied source interfaces, including their helpers. The baseline adds no perception or control modules beyond those interfaces. Geometry, Spatial Reasoning, Affordance, and Planning use Python runtime; Manipulation follows its native agent loop. Persistent variables let the agent build on earlier computations, while images produced during round enter the next model request. Appendix B.1 specifies the interfaces; the supplementary review study adds specialist measurements (Section 4.4) (Zhang et al., 2025, Huang et al., 2026d). Termination is distinct from success. Fixed-input submissions commit predictions. Interactive episodes end on agent termination, an environment terminal condition, budget exhaustion, or an unrecovered API or execution error. The evaluator then checks the submitted output or environment state independently of the agents declaration. Declaring completion therefore cannot substitute for satisfying the goal. The execution budgets are specified in Appendix B.2.

sections.content: We compare capability profiles, diagnose unmet task requirements, and examine how feedback changes predictions and execution.

sections.title: 4.2 Main Results
sections.content: Does perceptual strength predict execution success? Closed-weight models lead all five domains, with distinct profiles  (Table 2)  . ① Broad strengths. Astra and Gemini 4 Argon occupy the top two positions in Spatial Reasoning and Planning, and the top three in Manipulation (Figure 3). ② Selective strengths. Qwen-Max nearly matches Astra in Spatial Pass@1, 68.9% versus 69.4%, but completes 36.9% versus 80.3% of Planning tasks. Conversely, Opus 5.5 leads Manipulation at 47.8% while trailing Astra and Fable in Planning. Fixed-input questions assess supplied observation; interactive tasks additionally require choosing operations, tracking their effects, and meeting terminal condition. These demands distinguish perceptual competence from procedural and control competence. ③ Open-weight execution gaps. Qwen-397B, Qwen-27B, and DeepSeek-1017 achieve 48.051.6% Spatial Pass@1, but only 19.131.2% Planning and 9.920.9% Manipulation success. Variation among closed-weight models likewise shows that release category does not specify models execution strengths. Where does model diversity help? Planning overlap separates broadly shared success from model-specific and shared failures (Figure 7). ① Broadly shared success is concentrated. Only eight of 157 tasks are solved by all ten models; seven belong to symbolic VirtualHome. sections.title: 4.3 Diagnosing Unmet Task Requirements
sections.content: We distinguish errors in interpreting the observation, satisfying precise condition, and completing dependent actions through diagnostic measurements and traces (Figures 48). Geometry: which error remains after an apparently correct estimate? ① Scale bias and relative-shape error require different diagnoses. On GeoProbe depth, Gemini 4 and Qwen-397B have similar raw AbsRel, 0.299 and 0.312, but oracle scale alignment leaves 0.065 and 0.203. Gemini 4 has median predicted/true depth ratio below one in all sixty caserun observations; much of its metric error is common-scale component. The larger Qwen residual persists after per-case scalar rescaling. Astra combines 96.3% ordinal accuracy with 0.104 raw AbsRel, falling to 0.038 after alignment. Relative ordering, metric calibration, and residual shape thus separate models that single error average would group together. ② Camera sensitivity differs from motion-detection floor. With matched object interventions, Astra and Gemini 4 miss none of fifty moving observations under fixed camera, but miss 26 and 37 under large view change; neither falsely labels the stationary controls as moving. The additional errors therefore concern real object motion lost under camera change. In contrast, Qwen-27B misses all fifty moving observations in each camera condition. Its unchanged error is failure floor, not robustness to the perturbation (Appendix D.1). ③ Projected endpoints do not settle physical constraints. Fable finds no target in eight episodes; Astra and Gemini 4 record both proximity within 20 cm and sit action in five and seven, respectively (Table A27). On the same couch case, Gemini 4 and DeepSeek issue sit, then declare themselves seated and stop after 44 and 70 rounds; both fail the private native verifier. Here visible approach and an issued command do not establish the requested bodyobject relation. The trace establishes stopping misjudgment; the private verifier does not identify which pose or contact condition remained unmet. Aggregate first-goal success therefore hides both early and late attrition. ② Physical progress can be lost and rebuilt. The matched CALVIN sequence 0526 reveals one source of additional work. Opus and DeepSeek both finish under the same 40-round allowance, but use eighteen and 37 rounds. DeepSeek remains on block retrieval during rounds 1727: measured block height returns to about 2 cm after carrying attempt, and stacking begins only at round 28. Opus proceeds from retrieval at round 11 to stacking at round 13. The later subgoal inherits the actual object state left by preceding actions; an attempted carry can require renewed retrieval before the sequence advances. ③ Tool position and object state can Haojian Huang et al. On matched PlaceSphere, DeepSeek brings the gripper within 2.8 mm of its requested hover target, yet four later checks still return is_grasped=false; the sphere shifts away from its initial location. Contact-rich insertion imposes further constraints: Opus completes PickCube, PlaceSphere, and StackCube but fails PegInsertionSide and PlugCharger, whose charger criterion requires both 5 mm positional and 0.2 rad angular accuracy. sections.title: 4.4 When Feedback Changes the Outcome
sections.content: Feedback can change an answer, make code executable, or help achieve required state. We distinguish these outcomes before assessing the cost of further interaction. Does reconsideration repair the error that determines acceptance? The paired review records distinguish changes in semantics, coordinate validity, and task acceptance (Table A34). ① Corrections compete with regressions. On eighteen Spatial cases, Qwen-27Bs self-review fixes one wrong answer but changes two correct answers to wrong; crop review fixes two but breaks four. Both reviews change the correct back to left when judging which side of girl faces car. The net accuracy decrease therefore conceals genuine corrections alongside new reference-frame errors. Reinspection does not consistently preserve already-correct judgments. ② Valid coordinates are not sufficient grounding. Six of nine initial Affordance boxes extend beyond image bounds. Self-review repairs all six bounds violations, raising mean IoU from 0.034 to 0.152, yet no box reaches the 0.5 criterion. On RAGNet scene, the revised point reaches the functional mask, while an entirely out-of-image rectangle becomes an in-image box with IoU 0.447. This is concrete repair of representation validity, followed by remaining error in functional extent. ③ Mean improvement and accepted corrections can diverge. Tool-assisted review produces lower mean IoU of 0.145 but one accepted box; Astra also gains one accepted box. Thus broadly improved set of still-insufficient predictions can yield fewer accepted boxes than lower-mean set. The tool condition adds measurements and larger response allowance (Appendix E.2); its aggregate gain describes that combined procedure. Paired self-/crop-review examples and their exact changes appear in Appendix J.6. Which feedback repairs the actual execution bottleneck? ① Interface compliance consumes interaction opportunities. Qwen-Max records execution errors in 103/200 CALVIN rounds, including 95 syntax errors; Fable has syntax errors in 34/36 erroneous rounds (Table A44). Syntax-invalid responses cannot carry out their intended control program. Treating the resulting failures as physical reasoning errors would overlook opportunities lost before environment interaction. ② Valid execution can still leave control unresolved. Among thirty CALVIN episodes with an observed native prefix and no execution error, 24 fail: eleven achieve no subgoal, and thirteen achieve only part of the sequence. Likewise, 62/65 error-containing episodes later execute code successfully, but only three finish (Figure 8b). Code repair addresses an interface condition; it does not certify grasp, object placement, or subsequent subgoals. The PlaceSphere checks locate this distinction directly in the objects measured state. ③ Productive recovery restores prerequisite. On matched Archaeology Dating, Opus 5.5s first two rounds fail before any environment action. It then acquires tools, excavates three sites, reads artifact ages, and places the flag at the oldest site, completing in round seven; Gemini 4 finishes in eight (Figure A16). DeepSeek reaches score 0.5, but its final three rounds raise code errors without new environment steps. The successful trace connects each correction to evidence needed by the next decision, while the stalled trace receives no further environmental feedback. 13 Haojian Huang et al. In seven HumanCLAW traces, 98.2399.46% of reported tokens are prompt tokens, including the inputs processed for successive decisions. Gemini 4s unresolved plant search records 1.95M tokens across 73 executed rounds, with 48 turns and 24 translations; its action descriptions repeatedly report no plant found. The token total principally reflects repeated input processing during unsuccessful search. In other traces the model stops shortly after sitting attempt despite an unmet native condition. Search allocation and stopping assessment therefore require different diagnoses. ② The binding budget determines the next opportunity. DeepSeeks ScienceWorld animal search exhausts decision rounds with 89 environment steps unused. Conversely, Gemini 4s BEHAVIOR-1K toolbox attempt is blocked by the 640k-token ceiling after 37.5 minutes of 180-minute allowance. More wall time would admit neither next decision under the recorded protocol. Even successful episodes separate costs: on matched chair navigation, Gemini 4 uses seventeen rounds and 158k tokens versus DeepSeeks 65 and 938k, yet takes 437 versus 406 seconds. Progress per decision, token expenditure, and elapsed time must therefore be assessed separately against the resource that actually ends the attempt.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: Closed-weight models lead this five-domain evaluation, while open-weight VLMs show useful spatial reasoning but substantially lower Planning and Manipulation success. The deeper distinction lies in the errors behind the scores: scale bias and residual geometric distortion, region enclosure and valid action-point selection, and executable operations and achieved object states require different corrections. During longer sequences, lost physical progress may have to be recovered before the next subgoal becomes feasible. Feedback is useful when it resolves the particular requirement blocking progress. The matched traces show receiving-region correction completing an otherwise valid procedure and confirmed grasp enabling transport; they also show repeated valid code and unsupported stopping judgments leaving goals unmet. Token expenditure alone obscures this distinction. For Astra and Gemini 4, most failed tokens are concentrated in HumanCLAW, whereas unsuccessful attempts remain costly across other sources for the remaining models. Assessing frontier embodied agents therefore requires both complete-task outcomes and evidence of the state changes through which those outcomes are reached.

E.3 Native Capability and Complete Task Execution Native capability concerns the decisions model makes through an execution interface. Comparing robot-agent studies therefore requires identifying the task requirements, the perception and control capabilities supplied by the interface, and the resources available for completion. Together, these factors determine which parts of task completion depend on the models decisions. Context and supplied control capabilities. Robotic in-context learning uses demonstrations and interaction through context-conditioned policies, geometric transfer, world models, or skilland agent-based control (Huang et al., 2026b). Fixed model weights can therefore coexist with substantial execution support. Learned skill selection (Ahn et al., 2022), programmatic composition of perception and control APIs (Liang et al., 2022), and spatial value maps (Huang et al., 2023a) assign different responsibilities to the model and executor. GPT-Policy (Cheng et al., 2026) conditions fixed VLM on demonstrations, action references, and feedback, while constrained controller checks and executes its requests. Our baseline leaves task interpretation and action selection to the model through source-native helpers; the supplementary review study separately introduces specialist measurements. Task composition and execution support change the comparison. Our RoboCasa sample contains seven atomic and three composite tasks; RoboCasa365 contains three atomic and 53 Haojian Huang et al. Embodied Agent Arena seven composite tasks (Appendix A). PyRUA-Lean (Si et al., 2026) evaluates 18 atomic and 32 composite RoboCasa365 task types at five seeds each, with 86.7% and 39.4% success. Its Target50 selection differs from our pretrain-designated instances. Removing its frozen RLDX-1 policy lowers atomic and composite success to 65.6% and 20.0%, while retaining programmatic composition of other primitives. Execution allowances also differ: our RoboCasa protocols use 24 model rounds and 60 minutes of trial time; PyRUA-Lean uses 40 calls for atomic tasks, 100 for composite tasks, and two-hour watchdog. Both allow multiple actions per Python response. These settings evaluate different combinations of model reasoning, supplied control, and task demands. Interaction count and task success measure different outcomes. GPT-Policy (Cheng et al., 2026) reports 0/3 towel-pickup successes without demonstrations, averaging 96.3 decisions and 24.6 minutes. Human video raises success to 2/3 and lowers those averages to 76.7 decisions and 18.9 minutes, including failed trials. Our CALVIN analysis distinguishes further requirement: 62 error-containing episodes resume code execution, but only three complete the sequence (Appendix D.5.1). Resumed code execution and subsequent task success must therefore be measured separately. The required contact state must hold at verification. GPT-Policys plug task requires the plug to remain fully seated after release. Robot video yields 0/3 successes; adding aligned action references yields 2/3 (Cheng et al., 2026). Our within-task diagnostics expose related final-state requirements: initiation or arrival fails in 36 of Astras 37 unsuccessful traces, and five Astra HumanCLAW episodes record both proximity to the seat and sit action without satisfying the sitting condition. These examples distinguish predicted path or attempted action from satisfaction of its required endpoint or contact condition. The arena evaluates these requirements alongside final task success, interaction count, and elapsed time.
